tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestSkills
tools.description:
Render a card of standalone skills the user can add — org, shared, or Anthropic skills not yet enabled.

Call this when the task is one a skill could make repeatable — drafting in a house style, reviews against a playbook, a recurring workflow — and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about skills. Also when they ask for recommendations, or when ListSkills returned zero matches. Use ListSkills for skills they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a skill would help, or if you already rendered a suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Pass keywords drawn from the task itself, and set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). content.text:
You're right on both counts. Isaac isn't the tool for this, and the people should be abstract enough that their hands never "do" anything for real. Here's how the pieces fit.

## Why not Isaac or RL for the bodies

Isaac Lab trains physical motor control: balancing, walking, grasping with simulated joints. It's great for robots, and it's also why people in those demos look like wobbly ragdolls. For this game it would be:

- **Wrong layer:** the interesting question is *why* someone decided to knap flint, not *how* their fingers move.
- **Too expensive:** hundreds of agents living through generations at 100x speed can't each run a physics policy.
- **Uncontrollable:** you'd spend months getting someone to hold a rock.

So the body is **puppeted** and the mind is **simulated**. This is how The Sims, RimWorld, and Dwarf Fortress all work.

## Two layers, strictly separated

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SIMULATION (plain C#, no Unity dependency) │
│  agents, needs, knowledge, beliefs, world   │
│  ticks at any speed, can run headless       │
└──────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                   │ events: "Asha starts KNAP at rock#3, 40 min"
┌──────────────────▼──────────────────────────┐
│  PRESENTATION (Unity)                       │
│  picks animation, walks her there, plays    │
│  loop, spawns flakes particle, done         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The sim never knows animations exist. That means you can:

- Run 500 years headless in seconds to test whether agriculture ever emerges.
- Fast-forward in-game, where the presentation just skips or interpolates.
- Swap the art style later without touching the game logic.

## What an "agent" actually is

Each person is a bundle of data plus a decision loop:

- **Body:** age, health, hunger, fatigue, and simple heritable traits (strength, cold tolerance).
- **Personality:** a few sliders like curiosity, sociability, caution, and status-seeking.
- **Knowledge:** skills with a level, e.g. `knapping: 0.4`, `fire: 0.9`, `storage: 0.0`. Knowledge is per person, so if they die, it's gone.
- **Beliefs:** learned expectations like "gathering at the river in dry season → usually good" and "burning a goat → rain?".
- **Relationships:** kin, friends, and who they learn from.
- **Memory:** a short log of notable events, which also feeds the chronicle/myths later.

**Decisions use utility AI, not RL.** Every few in-game minutes, the agent scores the available **verbs** (gather, hunt, knap, cook, rest, socialize, teach, experiment, pray, migrate). Each score is roughly how badly they need it × how well they expect it to go × their personality. They pick one, probably with some randomness so they aren't robots. The Sims has run on essentially this model for 25 years, because it's cheap, readable, and debuggable.

## Where the ML actually sits

It sits in the **expectations**, not the bodies:

- **Each agent learns from experience.** After every action, they update what they expect it to produce in this context. That's a contextual bandit, basically a tiny Q-table per person. It's cheap and it's real learning.
- **Agents learn from each other.** They copy the expectations and skills of successful or high-status people, with copying errors. That's how culture, tradition, and superstition spread and drift.
- **The god-belief is the same machinery.** Your interventions are just another thing they try to predict.

This gives you non-scripted behavior at almost no compute cost. Unity ML-Agents *could* come in later for something narrow, like animal fleeing/herding behavior, but it's optional.

## Animation: a lookup, not ML

You don't need an animation-selector model. Each verb maps to a small set of clips:

| Verb | Clips |
|---|---|
| KNAP | sit + strike loop (3 variants) |
| GATHER | walk → crouch → pick loop → stand |
| SOCIALIZE | face partner, gesture/laugh loops |
| TEACH | same as the skill, plus a watcher playing "observe" |

A Unity Animator state machine or a simple C# script picks a clip from the verb, with a random variant. Hands only need to *look* right: IK snaps a prop to the hand bone, and a particle puff sells the flint strike. Mixamo or low-poly stylized characters are plenty.

## How it avoids feeling static

Static comes from **behavior** repeating, not from animation quality. What keeps this sim alive:

1. **Needs collide.** A hungry person who's also exhausted and grieving makes an odd choice, and you notice.
2. **Knowledge is uneven.** Only three people can make fire well, so everyone gathers around them. Social structure shows up on screen.
3. **Personality spreads outcomes.** Curious people waste time experimenting, and occasionally that's how pottery gets invented.
4. **The world changes:** seasons, herds migrating, a drought year.
5. **Cheap procedural polish:** agents look at whoever's talking, idles vary, walking paths spread out, kids follow parents. These are small touches, but they do most of the "alive" work.

## Level of detail for later

When you eventually zoom out to many societies, distant groups switch from individual agents to **aggregate stats** (population, skills distribution, beliefs). They switch back to individuals when you zoom in. Totally skippable for the one-valley prototype.

## One tick, concretely

> **Day 212, dry season.** Asha (curiosity 0.8, knapping 0.4) is hungry but the river roots came up empty the last two days, so her expected value for GATHER dropped. HUNT is low because she's never hunted. She scores EXPERIMENT high and picks it. She tries mixing river clay with ash near the fire and gets a 4% insight roll, which fails. Meanwhile Tomo watches her. He copies nothing because she didn't succeed, but her status drops slightly.
>
> **Presentation:** Asha walks to the fire, crouch-kneads a clay loop, and her thought bubble shows a question mark.

## Suggested path

1. **Headless sim first, maybe 1–2 weeks.** One valley on a grid, ~30 agents, 6–8 verbs, seasons, 3 discoverable techs (fire mastery, storage, pottery). Output a log plus charts. The only question it answers is whether emergence ever feels surprising.
2. **Unity with capsules.** Hook it to the event stream using colored capsules and floating icons. This is where you tune whether watching it is fun.
3. **Real art and animation** only after step 2 is fun.

For step 1 I could build a quick version right now, either a browser demo you can watch or a plain C# library you'd drop straight into Unity later. The C# option wastes less work since Unity is the target.

content.text:
Barely. Either machine is way more than this needs.

**Why it doesn't matter much:**
- **The simulation runs on the CPU.** Needs, utility scoring, and the little learning tables are just math on small numbers. A few hundred agents is trivial for any modern CPU, and even thousands is fine with a bit of care.
- **The "ML" I described is tiny.** Bandit tables and social copying need no GPU, no CUDA, and no training runs. Each agent learns during play.
- **Rendering low-poly people in a valley** is light work. Integrated graphics could probably handle the prototype.

**Where the GPU *would* matter later (all optional):**
- **A local LLM for myths/chronicles.** The 5080's 16GB of VRAM can comfortably run a ~8–14B model quantized. The 5070 laptop (8GB) can run smaller ~7–8B models. This is the one place the 5080 is clearly better.
- **Unity ML-Agents training**, if you ever train animal behaviors. Both cards handle it, and honestly most ML-Agents training is CPU-bound anyway.
- **Heavier visuals** if the art style gets ambitious (lots of foliage, lighting, crowds).

**Practical suggestion:** develop on whichever you like, and use the **laptop as your "minimum spec" test machine**. If it runs well there, it'll run well for most players.

What will matter for the prototype: a decent CPU (you almost certainly have one) and enough RAM to run Unity comfortably, so 16GB minimum and 32GB is nicer.

Want me to start on the headless C# sim? I'd set it up as a plain .NET project in this folder that you can run from the terminal now and drop into Unity later. That needs the .NET SDK installed. I can check whether you have it.

content.text:
You don't need Unity yet. Keep it installed and ready, but the first milestone works better without it.

I checked your PC:
- **Unity 6.3** (6000.3.9f1) is installed, which is good for later.
- **Git** is installed.
- **The .NET SDK is missing.** That's the one thing you need to install.

## Why skip Unity for now

The first question is whether the sim produces surprising emergence, and answering it means running hundreds of years in seconds, rerunning with different seeds, and reading logs and charts. Unity slows that loop down with domain reloads, play mode, and scene setup. A terminal app runs in about a second.

The trick is to write the sim **so that Unity can use it later unchanged**.

## The stack

| Thing | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Language | **C#** | Same language as Unity, so nothing gets rewritten |
| Runtime | **.NET SDK 8 or 10** | Builds and runs the sim from the terminal |
| Core library target | **netstandard2.1** | The format Unity 6 can load directly |
| Editor | **VS Code + C# Dev Kit**, or **JetBrains Rider** (free for non-commercial use) | Rider is excellent with Unity later |
| Version control | **Git** (already installed) | Commit early, since experiments will break things |
| Output | **CSV logs + a simple HTML chart viewer** | Lets you see population, skills, and beliefs over time |

## Project layout

```
Ideas and Thoughts/
└── Anthro/
    ├── Anthro.Sim/        ← core library (netstandard2.1): agents, world, verbs, learning
    │                         NO Unity references, ever
    ├── Anthro.Runner/     ← console app: "run 300 years, seed 42", writes logs/CSVs
    └── Anthro.Tests/      ← a few sanity tests (agents eat, people die, knowledge transfers)
```

Later, `Anthro.Sim` gets dropped into a Unity project (as a DLL or source folder), and Unity becomes just the viewer listening to sim events.

## What I'd build first, in order

1. **World:** a small grid valley with a river, plant patches that regrow by season, a clay deposit, flint, and a herd of one animal.
2. **Agents:** needs (hunger, fatigue, social), personality, skills, age and death, birth, and kinship.
3. **Verbs + utility AI:** gather, hunt, rest, socialize, knap, teach, experiment.
4. **Learning:** per-agent expected outcomes, plus copying from successful people.
5. **One emergent discovery chain:** fire mastery → storage → pottery, gated by real conditions.
6. **Runner output:** a readable chronicle ("Year 34: Asha's grandson is the last who can make pots") plus CSVs.

## Your one step

Install the .NET SDK. I can run this for you if you want:

```bash
winget install Microsoft.DotNet.SDK.8
```

Once it's installed, say go and I'll scaffold `Anthro/` and start on steps 1–3.

content.text:
I've set up only the parts we're sure of, and it builds cleanly.

```
Anthro/
├── Anthro.Sim/      ← sim library (Unity-compatible, no Unity code allowed)
├── Anthro.Runner/   ← console app for running it headless
├── Anthro.Tests/    ← tests
├── docs/PLANNING.md ← decisions log
└── README.md
```

I also installed the .NET 8 SDK and ran `git init`. Nothing is committed yet. There's no game code: the runner is still the default "Hello World".

[PLANNING.md](docs/PLANNING.md) has two lists. **Decided** holds only things you've explicitly agreed to, and right now that's just two lines (sim separate from Unity, start small). **Open** is everything else. Ideas I pitched stay Open until you confirm them.

## Things I filled in that you haven't agreed to

Here's what I'd put on the table so you can see what I assumed:

- The player is a god who **only acts through the environment** and can't give orders
- People form **religion by trying to predict you**
- Tech is **lost when the people who know it die**
- The real-world **domestication rules** (Diamond's criteria)
- People as utility-AI agents, using **verbs** like gather/knap/teach
- Prehistoric setting, starting with ~30 people in one valley
- No win condition / sandbox
- ML limited to small learning tables, with LLMs only for flavor

## How I'd run the planning session

We'd go in this order, because each topic shapes the ones after it:

1. **The fantasy:** what it should *feel* like to play, in one or two sentences, and what moment makes someone tell a friend about it.
2. **Your role:** god or not, what powers you have, and what your limits are.
3. **Scope of time and scale:** where it starts, how far it can go (stone age → bronze age? → modern?), one society or many.
4. **The core loop:** what you actually do minute to minute, and what you're watching for.
5. **Goals:** sandbox, scenarios, or a win/lose state.
6. **Systems:** evolution, domestication, knowledge, belief, conflict, trade. Which are core and which are later.
7. **Look & feel:** camera, art style, how much you see individuals.
8. **ML:** where it earns its place, now that the rest is defined.

After each topic I'll write what we agreed into PLANNING.md and show you, so nothing slips in silently.

## Topic 1: the fantasy

3. **How much should players care about individual people?** Like named characters with stories, or more like watching an ant colony?

If you're planning to search the web or internal knowledge bases, consider using this skill. This skill coordinates research subagents, so use it only when you have a tool for spawning subagents (the Agent or Task tool); otherwise, research the question directly.
- anthropic-skills:docs: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. - anthropic-skills:explain-usage: Explain where this session's tokens went, with one simple chart in plain language. Use when the user says things like "explain my usage", "where did my tokens go", or asks for a usage breakdown.

Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files.
- anthropic-skills:import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:schedule: Create or update a scheduled task that runs automatically. Use when the user says things like "every day", "each morning", "remind me in an hour", "run this at noon", or wants to reschedule an existing task.
- anthropic-skills:setup-claude: Guided setup — install role-matched plugins, connect your tools, try a skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- frontend-design:frontend-design: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. - code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. # Planning

Every big-picture call lives here. A decision is only **Decided** once it's
been explicitly agreed. Anything Claude suggested but wasn't confirmed stays
**Open**. Tensions are places where two stated goals pull against each other
and need a call.

## Why this game exists (your words, condensed)

Started from wondering how Native and other cultures might have developed
without colonization: whether people naturally discover certain things and
progress in certain ways (destiny vs. chance), and how varied and how similar
isolated cultures could become. An anthropological + biological evolution sim
about how cultures grow and advance, and how that shapes humanity itself.

## Decided

### Tech / process
- Core sim is plain C#, separate from Unity; Unity is a viewer later.
- Start small: prototype the sim headless before any visuals.

### Player role
- Player is a god-like figure who mostly **cannot interact directly**.
- Acts by shaping the world: placing animals, natural features, resources,
  plus other nudges.
- Occasionally a **prophet** appears, someone the player can actually talk to.
- People **misinterpreting the god** (religion forming from your actions) is
  a core moment.
- Some **pre-birth shaping of individuals** as an occasional opportunity
  (idea, mechanism TBD).
- Gameified to some extent, **while staying authentic**.

### Scale & progression
- Start small (one group), expand to **multiple societies** on islands /
  mini-continents that discover each other, eventually sailing between them.
- Loose arc toward a **modern-ish era**: steam engine, electricity are in scope.
- **Hidden pathways** underneath: not infinite possibilities, an invisible
  structure of tech routes the people can progress through.
- Blend of **sandbox + arc** (Civ 6-like loose direction).

### Feel
- **Garden, puzzle and drama** all present at different moments; drama is
  the smallest of the three.
- Failure is real: a disaster can kill your key inventor, and you may have to
  rebuild from survivors or restart with new humans.

### Systems in scope (priority not yet set)
- Biological evolution from a **predetermined set of trait pathways** we
  design (e.g. amphibious, hairy, gliding)
- Hunter-gatherer life, food, domestication
- Language development
- Hierarchies, economies, technologies
- Religions, beliefs, customs

### People
- Individuals matter; players will often pick favorites or heavily influence
  certain people.
- Personality depth around **Fallout Shelter** level.
- Loose **prewritten characters** that show up at different points and form
  a light story that is present but never forcing (Hades / Elden Ring style).

### Look & camera
- Default view shows **little people, not blobs** (Planet Zoo / Clash of Clans
  scale).
- Zoom out to the map/globe and travel to other islands/regions.
- Click a person or event for a close-up and deeper info (Planet Zoo style).
- Stylized indie art (Hades as a reference for the *quality* of stylization,
  not to copy).

### Story tone
- Mysterious and vague underlying lore (No Man's Sky style): present and cool,
  never dominating gameplay.

### Reference points
| Game | What we take from it |
|---|---|
| Planet Zoo | management style, scale/zoom, click-to-inspect |
| Fallout Shelter | personality depth of people |
| The Sims | making people feel natural despite simple animation |
| Hades | stylized art, how story is structured |
| No Man's Sky | discovery: figuring out how things work; mysterious lore |

## Tensions to resolve

1. **Destiny vs. pathways.** The founding question is *would* cultures
   naturally discover things? But hidden tech pathways + an arc toward modernity
   partly answer that question in advance. How convergent should outcomes be?
2. **Authentic vs. speculative biology.** Real anthropology (domestication,
   language, hierarchy) sits next to amphibious or gliding humans. How far into
   "what if" does evolution go?
3. **Individual people vs. thousands of years.** Watching named people live
   their lives, and reaching the steam engine, means spanning ~50,000+ years at
   human scale. How time works is a fundamental design call.
4. **What the player knows.** No Man's Sky discovery implies the *player* also
   learns what leads to what. Does the player see the hidden pathways, or
   discover them too?

## Open

- How powerful is the god, and what limits it (cost, cooldown, faith, none)?
- What the prophet can and can't do.
- How pre-birth shaping works.
- What happens on extinction (restart rules).
- What the mysterious lore *is* (who/what is the player?).
- System priority order.
- Where ML fits.
- Real Earth geography or invented worlds.
- Win / end conditions, if any.

I updated [PLANNING.md](docs/PLANNING.md) with everything you said under **Decided**, worded as closely to yours as I could. Read it over and tell me if I misheard anything.

There are four tensions in your vision. They're the most important calls in the whole design, because they shape everything else, so I'm putting them first. For each one I give my suggestion, labeled as such, and you decide.

## 1. Destiny vs. pathways

Your founding question is whether people naturally discover certain things. Hidden tech pathways and an arc toward modernity partly answer that in advance.

- **Convergent:** everyone eventually gets to bronze → iron → steam. It differs only in speed and order.
- **Contingent:** some cultures never get metallurgy. They might go deep on astronomy, or plant medicine, or seafaring instead. "Modern" could look very different across islands.

*My suggestion:* **many paths up the same mountain, with a few dead ends.** There are hidden pathways, but several routes to each milestone, and some cultures may plateau for good unless contact or the god breaks the deadlock. That keeps your "does destiny exist?" question open *in play*, and players will argue about it.

## 2. How speculative is the biology?

Domestication and language can be very grounded. Amphibious and gliding humans are "what if" territory.

*My suggestion:* **grounded rules, speculative outcomes.** Traits only evolve under real selection pressure over real-ish time. So island people who dive for food over thousands of years could get webbed hands, better breath-holding, and seal-like fat. Each trait pathway is plausible on its own, even if the end result looks alien. The authenticity lives in the *process*.

## 3. Individuals vs. 50,000 years (the big one)

You want to know named people *and* reach the steam engine. A human life is about 40 years, and the stone age alone is tens of thousands of years.

*Options:*
- **Time flows at variable speed:** you fast-forward through quiet centuries and the game slows down for key moments (a discovery is close, a prophet is born, a disaster hits). People become a blur and then come into focus again.
- **Eras as chapters:** each era plays at human scale, then time jumps hundreds or thousands of years, with a summary of what happened in between.
- **Generational focus:** you follow a lineage, so your "favorite person" becomes their great-great-grandchildren.

*My suggestion:* **variable speed plus lineages.** It fits your "I'd been watching this guy" moments and the garden/puzzle/drama mix.

## 4. Does the player know the pathways?

No Man's Sky's discovery feel implies the *player* figures things out too.

*My suggestion:* **the player discovers them alongside the people.** You start knowing nothing about what leads to pottery. You learn by watching, experimenting with nudges, and reading hints. A codex fills in as you learn. The fun is that players actually learn real anthropology by doing it.

---

Once these are settled, the next batch is the god's powers and limits, prophets, pre-birth shaping, and what happens on extinction. Take any of these four in any order, and push back hard on my suggestions if they don't feel right.

### Progression model (resolved tension 1)
- Discoveries are **authored events** (fire, windmill, steam engine...), not
  ML-invented. No heavy ML needed to make progression work.
- They form a **non-linear scatter**, not a tree; countless ways through it.
- **Contingent over convergent.** "Many paths up the same mountain" with some
  dead ends.
- **Many kinds of "advanced."** A culture can be clearly advanced without
  metallurgy or industry (Avatar's Pandora as a reference). Some branches can
  be **not 100% real** (plausible-feeling, speculative).
- Key discoveries are a **convergence of many conditions**. Getting everything
  to line up is the real difficulty and the core puzzle.

### Biology (resolved tension 2)
- **Grounded rules, speculative outcomes.** Traits evolve only under real-ish
  selection pressure over real-ish time; end results can look alien.

### Universal-ish systems
- **Language, domestication, and a food system** are near-universal (not
  guaranteed) with many routes to them, and get deeper, more thought-out
  systems than niche branches.

### Time (resolved tension 3)
- **Variable speed + lineages.** Time speeds through quiet stretches and slows
  for key moments; you follow families across generations.
- **No era structure.** Eras feel too linear.

- The player **discovers pathways alongside the people**. No objectives, no
  waypoint markers.
- Guidance comes from: a **codex** that fills in, **story/lore hints**, and the
  player's own modern-human common sense.
- Hints tell you loosely *what*; the challenge is making the convergence happen.
- Learning real anthropology through play is a goal.

- An **old god** who came before left hints. Explains why the player is a bit
  ahead of the people.

## Tensions to resolve

1. **What counts as "advanced"?** If Pandora-style and industrial cultures are
   both successful, the game needs some way to recognize it beyond tech count.

# Planning

Every big-picture call lives here. A decision is only **Decided** once it's
been explicitly agreed. Anything Claude suggested but wasn't confirmed stays
**Open**. Tensions are places where two stated goals pull against each other
and need a call.

## Why this game exists (your words, condensed)

Started from wondering how Native and other cultures might have developed
without colonization: whether people naturally discover certain things and
progress in certain ways (destiny vs. chance), and how varied and how similar
isolated cultures could become. An anthropological + biological evolution sim
about how cultures grow and advance, and how that shapes humanity itself.

## Decided

### Tech / process
- Core sim is plain C#, separate from Unity; Unity is a viewer later.
- Start small: prototype the sim headless before any visuals.

### Player role
- Player is a god-like figure who mostly **cannot interact directly**.
- Acts by shaping the world: placing animals, natural features, resources,
  plus other nudges.
- Occasionally a **prophet** appears, someone the player can actually talk to.
- People **misinterpreting the god** (religion forming from your actions) is
  a core moment.
- Some **pre-birth shaping of individuals** as an occasional opportunity
  (idea, mechanism TBD).
- Gameified to some extent, **while staying authentic**.

### Scale & progression
- Start small (one group), expand to **multiple societies** on islands /
  mini-continents that discover each other, eventually sailing between them.
- Loose arc toward a **modern-ish era**: steam engine, electricity are in scope.
- **Hidden pathways** underneath: not infinite possibilities, an invisible
  structure of tech routes the people can progress through.
- Blend of **sandbox + arc** (Civ 6-like loose direction).

### Feel
- **Garden, puzzle and drama** all present at different moments; drama is
  the smallest of the three.
- Failure is real: a disaster can kill your key inventor, and you may have to
  rebuild from survivors or restart with new humans.

### Systems in scope (priority not yet set)
- Biological evolution from a **predetermined set of trait pathways** we
  design (e.g. amphibious, hairy, gliding)
- Hunter-gatherer life, food, domestication
- Language development
- Hierarchies, economies, technologies
- Religions, beliefs, customs

### People
- Individuals matter; players will often pick favorites or heavily influence
  certain people.
- Personality depth around **Fallout Shelter** level.
- Loose **prewritten characters** that show up at different points and form
  a light story that is present but never forcing (Hades / Elden Ring style).

### Look & camera
- Default view shows **little people, not blobs** (Planet Zoo / Clash of Clans
  scale).
- Zoom out to the map/globe and travel to other islands/regions.
- Click a person or event for a close-up and deeper info (Planet Zoo style).
- Stylized indie art (Hades as a reference for the *quality* of stylization,
  not to copy).

### Story tone
- Mysterious and vague underlying lore (No Man's Sky style): present and cool,
  never dominating gameplay.

### Reference points
| Game | What we take from it |
|---|---|
| Planet Zoo | management style, scale/zoom, click-to-inspect |
| Fallout Shelter | personality depth of people |
| The Sims | making people feel natural despite simple animation |
| Hades | stylized art, how story is structured |
| No Man's Sky | discovery: figuring out how things work; mysterious lore |

## Tensions to resolve

1. **Destiny vs. pathways.** The founding question is *would* cultures
   naturally discover things? But hidden tech pathways + an arc toward modernity
   partly answer that question in advance. How convergent should outcomes be?
2. **Authentic vs. speculative biology.** Real anthropology (domestication,
   language, hierarchy) sits next to amphibious or gliding humans. How far into
   "what if" does evolution go?
3. **Individual people vs. thousands of years.** Watching named people live
   their lives, and reaching the steam engine, means spanning ~50,000+ years at
   human scale. How time works is a fundamental design call.
4. **What the player knows.** No Man's Sky discovery implies the *player* also
   learns what leads to what. Does the player see the hidden pathways, or
   discover them too?

## Open

- How powerful is the god, and what limits it (cost, cooldown, faith, none)?
- What the prophet can and can't do.
- How pre-birth shaping works.
- What happens on extinction (restart rules).
- What the mysterious lore *is* (who/what is the player?).
- System priority order.
- Where ML fits.
- Real Earth geography or invented worlds.
- Win / end conditions, if any.

I logged all four as decided in [PLANNING.md](docs/PLANNING.md), plus the old-god idea as a *leaning*, not final.

You're right that this doesn't need heavy ML. The "scatter of event tiles" can be fully authored and still produce countless paths. Here's how I picture one tile working, so we can make sure we mean the same thing, since this is the backbone of the game.

## What a discovery tile looks like

**Example: Bow and arrow**

| Condition type | Requirement | Ways to satisfy it |
|---|---|---|
| Material | springy wood | yew, ash, *or* bamboo, *or* horn + sinew composite |
| Material | string | sinew (needs hunting), *or* plant fiber (needs cordage) |
| Knowledge | cordage | its own tile |
| Knowledge | projectile hunting | spear-throwing *or* atlatl |
| Pressure | a reason | fast/wary prey, *or* conflict with neighbors |
| Person | the right individual | someone curious who's skilled at hunting *or* woodwork, and who happens to be in the right situation |

When every row is satisfied, the discovery **becomes possible, not guaranteed**. It gets a chance each time a qualifying person does a related activity. Then it has to **spread** through teaching, or it dies with them.

Here's why this produces countless paths:
- **OR-options** mean different cultures arrive by different routes. A bamboo-and-plant-fiber bow culture really does differ from a horn-and-sinew one, and that flavor can carry forward.
- **Tiles feed tiles**, so the "scatter" is really a big web where some tiles are reachable from many directions.
- **Pressures** mean a comfortable culture may *never* bother, even with all the materials. That's your dead ends and your Pandora-style divergence.
- **Your role as god** is to push missing rows into place: plant bamboo, send fast antelope, nudge a curious kid's birth. Then you hope.

Does that match what you picture? This one is worth a firm yes or a correction.

## Tension: what counts as "advanced"?

If a Pandora-like culture and an industrial one are both "successful," the game needs to recognize that somehow, even without a win screen. A few options:

- **Dimensions instead of a score:** for example *mastery of nature, knowledge, wellbeing, reach (how far they travel/influence), complexity (social/technical), and continuity (how long the culture's lasted)*. Cultures come out as different shapes, like a radar chart.
- **Milestones of a different kind:** "first to sail to another island," "first written record," "a city of 10,000," "lived 1,000 years without famine." These can be reached in many ways.
- **No judgment at all:** the game just describes cultures, and you decide what you're proud of.

*My suggestion:* dimensions + milestones. That honors many kinds of success without crowning a winner. What do you think?

## Next batch: the god's hands

1. **Powers:** what do you imagine being able to do? Your list so far is placing animals, natural features, resources, nudges, prophets, and pre-birth shaping. Anything bigger (earthquakes, plagues, climate shifts), or deliberately not?
2. **Limits:** should powers be **free**, or cost something? Some options:
   - a **faith/belief currency**: the more people believe in you, the more you can do, which ties into the misinterpretation mechanic
   - **cooldowns**
   - **natural consequences only**: you can do anything, but the ecosystem reacts, e.g. drop in wolves and they eat your deer
3. **Prophet:** how do you picture talking to them? Picking from a few messages? Typing freely (this is where an LLM could really fit)? And do they get your message right, or garble it?
4. **Pre-birth shaping:** how often does it come up, and what can you shape? Personality, talents, physical traits?
5. **Extinction:** if everyone dies, do you restart in the same world, which keeps your changes to animals and land, or start fresh? Is there a way to lose the whole game?

### Discovery tiles
- Each tile has condition rows: **materials, knowledge, pressure, person**.
  Rows can be satisfied by **alternatives (OR)**, so cultures arrive by
  different routes and carry that flavor forward.
- All rows met = discovery **possible, not guaranteed**; it rolls when a
  qualifying person does related activity, then must **spread** or die out.
- The god's job is pushing missing rows into place.
- The full web gets **drawn out** as its own design step.

### Advancement & success (resolved)
- **Dimensions + milestones**, no single score.
- Any flavor of society can **keep advancing** with clearly forward unlocks
  (Pandora-style included), so players feel it thriving.
- When a flavor is **maxed out**, the game acknowledges you've perfected it.

### People's minds
- Each person's mind is a **map**: beliefs, learned things, traits, interests,
  disposition, stats, abilities.
- That map gates which tiles they can trigger **and** drives their activity
  choices, learning ML-style.
- Clicking a person shows **current thoughts** and a cool visual of this
  mind map.

### God powers
- Base kit: place animals, natural features, resources; nudges; prophet;
  pre-birth shaping; life branch-point nudges.
- **Big events** (earthquakes, plagues, climate) exist but are sparing and
  limited, and some come later.
- Story frame: **you just became a god** and are figuring it out.
- Powers **unlock** over time via:
  - **belief** (how many believe, and how strongly)
  - **how you're perceived**: a malevolent god gets different powers/options
    than a benevolent one
  - **story progression**
  - possibly a god skill tree (visible or hidden, undecided)
- **Atheism weakens you.** Rival / false gods: maybe.
- God story progression and society progression are separate, but tied
  together through religion.
- **Natural consequences** happen, scoped carefully to stay buildable.

### Prophet / vessel
- More **vessel/directed** than conversational: a fully obedient prophet.
- Ideally **free typing**; possibly options that depend on context/location.
- The prophet gets your message **right**; the people who hear it may not.
  Belief can drift from your intent (Israelites-in-the-desert style).

### Shaping individuals
- **Pre-birth:** can shape personality, talents, physical traits.
- **Life branch points:** you get a notification when someone hits a fork that
  will shape their life, and can push them one way.

### Failure & restart
- Hard loss candidates: **extinction**, maybe **losing all believers**.
- **Soft failure:** a society locked into a bad direction (e.g. stagnant
  authoritarian) that can't advance; you must change a lot, even regress, to
  move forward.
- On extinction: **mold new humans in the same world** or start a new game.
  How long you wait sets what's left: recent ruins (like Rome) vs. fossils
  (like dinosaurs).

### Biology (resolved tension 2)

# Planning

Every big-picture call lives here. A decision is only **Decided** once it's
been explicitly agreed. Anything Claude suggested but wasn't confirmed stays
**Open**. Tensions are places where two stated goals pull against each other
and need a call.

## Why this game exists (your words, condensed)

Started from wondering how Native and other cultures might have developed
without colonization: whether people naturally discover certain things and
progress in certain ways (destiny vs. chance), and how varied and how similar
isolated cultures could become. An anthropological + biological evolution sim
about how cultures grow and advance, and how that shapes humanity itself.

## Decided

### Tech / process
- Core sim is plain C#, separate from Unity; Unity is a viewer later.
- Start small: prototype the sim headless before any visuals.

### Player role
- Player is a god-like figure who mostly **cannot interact directly**.
- Acts by shaping the world: placing animals, natural features, resources,
  plus other nudges.
- Occasionally a **prophet** appears, someone the player can actually talk to.
- People **misinterpreting the god** (religion forming from your actions) is
  a core moment.
- Some **pre-birth shaping of individuals** as an occasional opportunity
  (idea, mechanism TBD).
- Gameified to some extent, **while staying authentic**.

### Scale & progression
- Start small (one group), expand to **multiple societies** on islands /
  mini-continents that discover each other, eventually sailing between them.
- Loose arc toward a **modern-ish era**: steam engine, electricity are in scope.
- **Hidden pathways** underneath: not infinite possibilities, an invisible
  structure of tech routes the people can progress through.
- Blend of **sandbox + arc** (Civ 6-like loose direction).

### Feel
- **Garden, puzzle and drama** all present at different moments; drama is
  the smallest of the three.
- Failure is real: a disaster can kill your key inventor, and you may have to
  rebuild from survivors or restart with new humans.

### Systems in scope (priority not yet set)
- Biological evolution from a **predetermined set of trait pathways** we
  design (e.g. amphibious, hairy, gliding)
- Hunter-gatherer life, food, domestication
- Language development
- Hierarchies, economies, technologies
- Religions, beliefs, customs

### People
- Individuals matter; players will often pick favorites or heavily influence
  certain people.
- Personality depth around **Fallout Shelter** level.
- Loose **prewritten characters** that show up at different points and form
  a light story that is present but never forcing (Hades / Elden Ring style).

### Look & camera
- Default view shows **little people, not blobs** (Planet Zoo / Clash of Clans
  scale).
- Zoom out to the map/globe and travel to other islands/regions.
- Click a person or event for a close-up and deeper info (Planet Zoo style).
- Stylized indie art (Hades as a reference for the *quality* of stylization,
  not to copy).

### Story tone

  never dominating gameplay.

| Fallout Shelter | personality depth of people |

# Planning

Every big-picture call lives here. A decision is only **Decided** once it's
been explicitly agreed. Anything Claude suggested but wasn't confirmed stays
**Open**. Tensions are places where two stated goals pull against each other
and need a call.

## Why this game exists (your words, condensed)

Started from wondering how Native and other cultures might have developed
without colonization: whether people naturally discover certain things and
progress in certain ways (destiny vs. chance), and how varied and how similar
isolated cultures could become. An anthropological + biological evolution sim
about how cultures grow and advance, and how that shapes humanity itself.

## Decided

### Tech / process
- Core sim is plain C#, separate from Unity; Unity is a viewer later.
- Start small: prototype the sim headless before any visuals.

### Player role
- Player is a god-like figure who mostly **cannot interact directly**.
- Acts by shaping the world: placing animals, natural features, resources,
  plus other nudges.
- Occasionally a **prophet** appears, someone the player can actually talk to.
- People **misinterpreting the god** (religion forming from your actions) is
  a core moment.
- Some **pre-birth shaping of individuals** as an occasional opportunity
  (idea, mechanism TBD).
- Gameified to some extent, **while staying authentic**.

### Scale & progression
- Start small (one group), expand to **multiple societies** on islands /
  mini-continents that discover each other, eventually sailing between them.
- Loose arc toward a **modern-ish era**: steam engine, electricity are in scope.
- **Hidden pathways** underneath: not infinite possibilities, an invisible
  structure of tech routes the people can progress through.
- Blend of **sandbox + arc** (Civ 6-like loose direction).

### Feel
- **Garden, puzzle and drama** all present at different moments; drama is
  the smallest of the three.
- Failure is real: a disaster can kill your key inventor, and you may have to
  rebuild from survivors or restart with new humans.

### Systems in scope (priority not yet set)
- Biological evolution from a **predetermined set of trait pathways** we
  design (e.g. amphibious, hairy, gliding)
- Hunter-gatherer life, food, domestication
- Language development
- Hierarchies, economies, technologies
- Religions, beliefs, customs

### People
- Individuals matter; players will often pick favorites or heavily influence
  certain people.
- Personality depth around **Fallout Shelter** level.
- Loose **prewritten characters** that show up at different points and form
  a light story that is present but never forcing (Hades / Elden Ring style).

### Look & camera
- Default view shows **little people, not blobs** (Planet Zoo / Clash of Clans
  scale).
- Zoom out to the map/globe and travel to other islands/regions.
- Click a person or event for a close-up and deeper info (Planet Zoo style).
- Stylized indie art (Hades as a reference for the *quality* of stylization,
  not to copy).

### Story tone
- Mysterious and vague underlying lore (No Man's Sky style): present and cool,
  never dominating gameplay.

### Reference points
| Game | What we take from it |
|---|---|
| Planet Zoo | management style, scale/zoom, click-to-inspect |
| Fallout Shelter | personality depth of people |
| The Sims | making people feel natural despite simple animation |
| Hades | stylized art, how story is structured |
| No Man's Sky | discovery: figuring out how things work; mysterious lore |

### Progression model (resolved tension 1)
- Discoveries are **authored events** (fire, windmill, steam engine...), not
  ML-invented. No heavy ML needed to make progression work.
- They form a **non-linear scatter**, not a tree; countless ways through it.
- **Contingent over convergent.** "Many paths up the same mountain" with some
  dead ends.
- **Many kinds of "advanced."** A culture can be clearly advanced without
  metallurgy or industry (Avatar's Pandora as a reference). Some branches can
  be **not 100% real** (plausible-feeling, speculative).
- Key discoveries are a **convergence of many conditions**. Getting everything
  to line up is the real difficulty and the core puzzle.

### Discovery tiles
- Each tile has condition rows: **materials, knowledge, pressure, person**.
  Rows can be satisfied by **alternatives (OR)**, so cultures arrive by
  different routes and carry that flavor forward.
- All rows met = discovery **possible, not guaranteed**; it rolls when a
  qualifying person does related activity, then must **spread** or die out.
- The god's job is pushing missing rows into place.
- The full web gets **drawn out** as its own design step.

### Advancement & success (resolved)
- **Dimensions + milestones**, no single score.
- Any flavor of society can **keep advancing** with clearly forward unlocks
  (Pandora-style included), so players feel it thriving.
- When a flavor is **maxed out**, the game acknowledges you've perfected it.

### People's minds
- Each person's mind is a **map**: beliefs, learned things, traits, interests,
  disposition, stats, abilities.
- That map gates which tiles they can trigger **and** drives their activity
  choices, learning ML-style.
- Clicking a person shows **current thoughts** and a cool visual of this
  mind map.

### God powers
- Base kit: place animals, natural features, resources; nudges; prophet;
  pre-birth shaping; life branch-point nudges.
- **Big events** (earthquakes, plagues, climate) exist but are sparing and
  limited, and some come later.
- Story frame: **you just became a god** and are figuring it out.
- Powers **unlock** over time via:
  - **belief** (how many believe, and how strongly)
  - **how you're perceived**: a malevolent god gets different powers/options
    than a benevolent one
  - **story progression**
  - possibly a god skill tree (visible or hidden, undecided)
- **Atheism weakens you.** Rival / false gods: maybe.
- God story progression and society progression are separate, but tied
  together through religion.
- **Natural consequences** happen, scoped carefully to stay buildable.

### Prophet / vessel
- More **vessel/directed** than conversational: a fully obedient prophet.
- Ideally **free typing**; possibly options that depend on context/location.
- The prophet gets your message **right**; the people who hear it may not.
  Belief can drift from your intent (Israelites-in-the-desert style).

### Shaping individuals
- **Pre-birth:** can shape personality, talents, physical traits.
- **Life branch points:** you get a notification when someone hits a fork that
  will shape their life, and can push them one way.

### Failure & restart
- Hard loss candidates: **extinction**, maybe **losing all believers**.
- **Soft failure:** a society locked into a bad direction (e.g. stagnant
  authoritarian) that can't advance; you must change a lot, even regress, to
  move forward.
- On extinction: **mold new humans in the same world** or start a new game.
  How long you wait sets what's left: recent ruins (like Rome) vs. fossils
  (like dinosaurs).

### Biology (resolved tension 2)
- **Grounded rules, speculative outcomes.** Traits evolve only under real-ish
  selection pressure over real-ish time; end results can look alien.

### Universal-ish systems
- **Language, domestication, and a food system** are near-universal (not
  guaranteed) with many routes to them, and get deeper, more thought-out
  systems than niche branches.

### Time (resolved tension 3)
- **Variable speed + lineages.** Time speeds through quiet stretches and slows
  for key moments; you follow families across generations.
- **No era structure.** Eras feel too linear.

### Player knowledge (resolved tension 4)
- The player **discovers pathways alongside the people**. No objectives, no
  waypoint markers.
- Guidance comes from: a **codex** that fills in, **story/lore hints**, and the
  player's own modern-human common sense.
- Hints tell you loosely *what*; the challenge is making the convergence happen.
- Learning real anthropology through play is a goal.

### Lore leaning (not final)
- An **old god** who came before left hints. Explains why the player is a bit
  ahead of the people.

## Tensions to resolve

1. **What counts as "advanced"?** If Pandora-style and industrial cultures are
   both successful, the game needs some way to recognize it beyond tech count.

## Open

- How powerful is the god, and what limits it (cost, cooldown, faith, none)?
- What the prophet can and can't do.
- How pre-birth shaping works.
- What happens on extinction (restart rules).
- What the mysterious lore *is* beyond the old-god leaning.
- System priority order.
- Where ML fits.
- Real Earth geography or invented worlds.
- Win / end conditions, if any.

content.text:
All logged in [PLANNING.md](docs/PLANNING.md). Your answers raised two technical tensions, both about where ML fits, so they're worth settling before anything else.

## Tension 1: the mind map, learned vs. legible

Your brain-map idea is the right place for ML, and it's a natural fit. The catch is that a deep neural net is a black box. You couldn't draw it as a readable mind map, you couldn't say why someone did something, and pre-birth shaping would have nothing clear to grab onto.

*My suggestion:* **the mind is a learned graph.**
- **Nodes** are readable things: `fire`, `river`, `the god`, `wolves`, `Asha`, `storing food`, `curiosity`.
- **Links** carry learned weights: "fire → warmth +0.9", "burning goats → rain +0.4 (wrong, but believed)", "Asha → trustworthy +0.7".
- **Learning** happens from experience (things that happen together get linked), from being taught, and from copying others. This is real, well-studied learning. It's just not deep learning.
- **Choices** come from scoring activities using the graph plus needs and personality.
- **The visual you wanted** falls straight out of this: a glowing web of a person's mind, with strong beliefs bright and fading ones dim. Current thoughts are whichever nodes are lit up right now.
- **Shaping** becomes concrete: pre-birth, you set trait nodes. At a branch point, you strengthen one link.

It's cheap enough to run for thousands of people, and every behavior is explainable. If we later want a neural piece for something narrow, it can plug in, but I wouldn't build the core on one.

## Tension 2: the free-typed prophet

Free typing works well if the LLM is only a **translator**. You type "tell them to stop burning the forest and plant seeds by the river." The LLM turns that into structured commands the sim understands (`TEACH: planting @ river`, `FORBID: burning @ forest`) and writes the prophet's sermon text. The sim never depends on the LLM's judgment.

The open questions are practical:
- **Cloud API:** best quality, but costs money per use and needs internet.
- **Local model:** free and offline. Your 5080 handles it fine, but weaker PCs struggle.
- **Fallback:** contextual menu options always exist, so it works without an LLM.

*My suggestion:* design it menu-first, with free typing layered on top. Decide cloud vs. local much later.

## Your open questions

**Pre-birth frequency:** tie it to belief, so it's a limited power. For example, a few "blessed births" per generation, more if belief is strong. Prophet lineages and devout families might offer them more often. That makes it scarce and meaningful, which fits "I engineered this kid and waited 20 years."

**Natural consequences, keeping it buildable:**
- **In:** predator-prey populations, plant regrowth, overhunting, soil exhaustion, disease spreading through dense settlements. All of these can be built.
- **Out (or faked):** real climate or fluid simulation. Big climate events are scripted effects with simple rules.

## Next batch: the core loop and the world

These matter most for what we build first.

1. **What does a typical 10 minutes of play look like?** For example: watch the camp, notice people are cold and hungry in winter, open the codex, see a hint about storing food, place clay by the river, wait, a kid starts playing with the clay, a notification says they're at a branch point, you push them... Describe it however you see it.
2. **World:** a real Earth-like map, or **invented** islands/continents generated per game? Procedural generation means every game is different.
3. **Starting point:** do you start with already-modern-ish humans (*Homo sapiens* bands), or earlier hominins that evolution can take in odd directions?
4. **Priority:** now that you've seen how things fit, which 2–3 systems feel most essential to prove the game is fun? My guess is **people's minds + discovery tiles + god nudges**, with evolution, language, and multi-society later. But this is your call.

content.text:
First, how traits and interests drive decisions, since that's the heart of the people system. Then the visuals, then a full relay of everything with the gaps I found.

## 1. How traits, interests, and lessons all shape decisions

Learned lessons are just one layer. A person's mind has several layers that change at different speeds:

| Layer | Examples | Changes | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Traits** | curiosity, caution, sociability, patience, aggression, dexterity | almost never | genes + pre-birth shaping |
| **Interests** | stone, animals, plants, sky, spirits, people, water | slowly, over years | enjoyment, mentors, childhood experiences |
| **Skills** | knapping 0.6, tracking 0.2 | through practice | doing and being taught |
| **Beliefs / lessons** | "river roots fail in dry season," "the god likes fire" | constantly | experience, teaching, copying others |
| **Relationships** | trusts Asha, fears Tomo | constantly | interactions |
| **State** | hungry, grieving, afraid, inspired | minute to minute | body + events |
| **Culture** (shared) | taboos, customs, what's "proper" | across generations | the group's shared beliefs |

**When choosing an activity, each layer pulls differently:**

```
score = need it solves         (hunger makes FORAGE urgent)
      × expected result        (beliefs: "foraging at the river works")
      + interest bonus         (she likes plants, so it's rewarding in itself)
      + trait pulls            (curious → EXPERIMENT, cautious → avoids HUNT)
      + social pull            (friends are going; elder told her to)
      − culture                (taboo: nobody forages the burial grove)
      + a bit of randomness
```

**Traits also change how people learn**, which is where it gets interesting:
- **Cautious** people weight bad outcomes heavily, so one wolf attack makes them avoid the forest for years.
- **Stubborn** people barely update beliefs. They keep old superstitions longer, which is great for tradition and bad for progress.
- **Sociable** people copy others more. **Curious** people try untested things.
- **Interests grow from enjoyment.** A kid who loves stone and has a patient knapper grandfather becomes the specialist, and specialists are who trigger discovery tiles.

**Example: same situation, different people.** Winter, food is low.
- **Asha** (curious, likes plants) experiments with drying berries by the fire. → She could trigger *food preservation*.
- **Tomo** (bold, likes animals, good tracker) goes on a risky hunt.
- **Elder Ren** (cautious, stubborn, devout) organizes a ritual, because "last time we burned a goat, the snow stopped."

All three are reasonable choices from their minds, and the camp suddenly feels like real people. Does this layering match what you imagined?

## 2. Visuals and perspective (not decided, here are the trade-offs)

| Option | Feel | Cost / risk |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Full 3D free camera** (Sims, Planet Zoo) | most immersive close-ups | highest: animation, terrain, and camera all have to look good from every angle, which is where jank shows |
| **B. Stylized 3D, guided camera** (Timberborn, Against the Storm, Townscaper) | tilted view, rotate/zoom, little readable people, can still zoom in close | moderate: stylization hides simple animation, and the camera limits avoid ugly angles |
| **C. Hades-style painted pseudo-3D** | gorgeous | very high art cost: every body shape and animation hand-drawn. **Evolution makes this explode**, because webbed or hairy or gliding people all need redrawn art |
| **D. 2D top-down** (RimWorld) | cheapest | loses the "see little people up close" feel you want |

**The deciding factor is evolution.** Changing bodies are far easier in 3D: swap parts, morph shapes, change hair/skin via shaders. That points strongly to 3D. *My suggestion:* **B, stylized low-poly 3D with a guided camera**, plus a close-up "inspect" mode. Zooming out turns into a **stylized map view** (like a painted chart) instead of a seamless globe, which is far easier to build. Look up **Timberborn** in particular: management-scale, stylized 3D, little characters, and it looks great without complex animation.

## 3. Full relay

I rewrote [PLANNING.md](docs/PLANNING.md) as one organized design doc so it's all in one place. Here are the parts I most want you to check: things we haven't talked about at all.

5. **Discover alongside them.** The player learns how humanity works by playing.

  relationships · state (moment) · culture (shared, generational).

  stubborn = updates slowly; sociable = copies more).

  pray...) mapped to animations; the Sims approach to natural-looking people.

- Hunter-gatherer life
- Hierarchies, economies, technologies

  tragedies should trace back to something the player could have seen coming.

  what remains: recent ruins (Rome) vs. fossils (dinosaurs).

4. **People are minds.** Individuals with traits, interests and beliefs drive everything.
5. **Discover alongside them.** The player learns how humanity works by playing.

  limited, and some unlock later.
- Powers **unlock** via belief (count and strength), how you're perceived
  (malevolent vs. benevolent gods get different options), and story progression.
- **Atheism weakens you.**
- God progression and society progression are separate but linked through religion.

**Prophet / vessel**

  drift from your intent.
- **Start with contextual menu options.** Free typing later, with an LLM as a
  **translator only** (text → structured sim commands + sermon text).

  prophet lineages / devout families may offer more.
